top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) best meets the common criteria. It pairs an explanatory framework (the supply-and-demand account of the skill premium and tasks) with design-based local-labour-market evidence on trade exposure. The work is mature, with the skill-premium line about three decades old, the task framework over two decades and the China-shock papers over a decade. It has been replicated and criticised, and the dispute concerns magnitude and persistence, not whether the effects exist. Katz's wage-structure line supplies the interpretive frame that makes the trade evidence a statement about labour demand. The citation should say only what has been shown and should not claim origination of the task model or restate the 2023 and 2024 prizes. Katz is the most exposed name because of his work with Goldin, and Dorn's exclusion is a cost of the three-name cap. P002 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) is a defensible, narrower single-discovery alternative that I rank second and would accept. Both beat no award because B006 is a substantial, well-confirmed achievement. The convergence of ten of eleven round-2 files is not evidence of merit and did not drive this ranking.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile for Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn. I disclose field proximity, since my social-mobility research is topically near B050, where Katz is also credited, but B050 is not in the slate. I also disclose long-standing IIES and co-author ties to Krusell and Boppart, who support P001, so their agreement is not independent confirmation.
